## Data download from Linked Omics

RNA-sequencing dataset contains gene expression measurements from <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Liver</strong></span> cancer samples. 
```{r}
#data_rna10 <- TCGAbiolinks::getLinkedOmicsData(project = "TCGA-LIHC", dataset = "RNAseq (HiSeq, Gene level)")

#saveRDS(data_rna10, "Liver_rna.rds")

data_rna = readRDS("Liver_rna.rds")
```

### Dataset

Each row represents a gene, and the expression measurements for the patients are stored in the other columns.

```{r}
head(data_rna[,1:7])
```

## Data pre-processing

Not all of genes are equally useful when we compare patients. 

- We will first remove genes with low average expression. <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Genes</strong></span> with a <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>mean expression</strong></span> ≥ 10 were retained, 

- We will keep the genes that change the most across patients. The goal is to build our network using a smaller set of informative expression profiles. The <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Top 20%</strong></span> with the highest coefficient of variation (CV) genes were selected.

### Selection of expressed genes

Selection of patient columns:
```{r, message=FALSE, warning= FALSE}
library(dplyr)

rna_samples <- data_rna %>%
  select(-attrib_name)
```

Calculate mean expression for each gene.
 
 - We separate the gene names from the numerical measurements, to use `rowMeans()` function. We calculate the mean expression of every gene across patients. 
```{r}
mean_expression <- rowMeans(rna_samples, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Remotion of genes with mean expression $<$ 10
```{r}
rna_mean_filtered <- data_rna[mean_expression >= 10, ]

rna_samples_filtered <- rna_samples[mean_expression >= 10, ]
```


### Selection of most informative genes
We selected the most informative genes across the patients with the `Coefficient of Variation`.

The coefficient of variation is calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the mean. 

- We rank the genes by CV and select the top 20% genes.
```{r}
#Calculate the coefficient of variation (CV)
gene_mean <- rowMeans(rna_samples_filtered, na.rm = TRUE)

gene_sd <- apply(
  rna_samples_filtered,
  1,
  sd,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

cv <- gene_sd / gene_mean
```

Rank genes from highest to lowest CV:
```{r}
gene_order <- order(
  cv,
  decreasing = TRUE,
  na.last = NA)
```

Keep the top 20% most variable genes
```{r}
n_top <- ceiling(length(gene_order) * 0.20)

selected_genes <- head(gene_order, n_top)

rna_filtered <- rna_mean_filtered[selected_genes, ]
```

## Network construction

The dataset is the starting point of che network analysis. 
In this first network, <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Nodes:</strong></span>. We connect two patients when their gene expression profiles are sufficiently similar, according to <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Pearson correlation</strong></span>. 

- The correlation value is the weight of the connection.


### Similarity of patient
High positive correlation means that their patterns tend to change together. The function `cor()` compares the columns, which are our patients. We also set the diagonal to zero because we do not want self loops.

- Use of the `cor()` function
```{r}
library(igraph)

rna_data <- rna_filtered[, 2:372]

rna_similarity <- cor(
  rna_data,
  method = "pearson")

diag(rna_similarity) <- 0 #no self loops

```

### Creation of edgelist

The correlation matrix contains a value for every pair of patients. Because Pearson correlation is symmetric, we only take the lower triangle so that we count every pair once.

```{r}
edge_index <- which(
  lower.tri(rna_similarity, diag = FALSE),
  arr.ind = TRUE)

head(edge_index)


#lower.tri() returns TRUE for those located below the main diagonal.

#which() finds all cells that contain TRUE, and arr.ind = TRUE returns two numbers: the row and the column.

#In this way we have a matrix that tells you where to retrieve the values corresponding to the pairs.
```

Construction of a dataframe that contains the pairs similarity:
```{r}
rna_all_edges <- data.frame(
  from = colnames(rna_similarity)[edge_index[, 1]],
  to = colnames(rna_similarity)[edge_index[, 2]],
  weight = rna_similarity[edge_index])
#in this way we can have dataframe that has an edgelist form
```


We don't want a complete graph. We define a <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>**similarity threshold**:</strong></span> patients, below which the edge weight is set to **0**.

- The 85th quantile is selected with `quantile()` function.
```{r}
similarities <- rna_similarity[lower.tri(rna_similarity)]

threshold <- quantile(
  similarities,
  0.85,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

```

Keep only similarities above the threshold.

- Similarities under the threshold are forced to 0.
```{r}
rna_adjacency <- rna_similarity

rna_adjacency[rna_adjacency < threshold] <- 0 

diag(rna_adjacency) <- 0
```

Weighted RNA network with `igraph`.
```{r}
rna_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
  rna_adjacency,
  mode = "upper",
  diag = FALSE,
  weighted = TRUE
)

rna_graph <- delete_edges(
  rna_graph,
  E(rna_graph)[E(rna_graph)$weight == 0])
```

### Graph edge weights distribution
We can build a histogram of the edge weights starting from an igraph object.
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(
  data.frame(weight = E(rna_graph)$weight),
  aes(x = weight)
) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    x = "Edge weight",
    y = "Frequency",
    title = "Distribution of RNA edge weights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```


## Comparison of the network communities

We want to compare two community detection analysis: <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Walktrap</strong></span> and <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Louvain</strong></span>**. 

We use <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>robin</strong></span> package, with the function `robinCompare()` to perturb the network gradually and check how much the detected communities change. .

- At increasing levels of graph perturbation, the community structures detected by the same method on the unperturbed and perturbed graphs are compared, generating a robustness curve.
```{r, message=FALSE}
library(robin)

graph = rna_graph

comparison = robinCompare(graph=graph, method1="walktrap", method2="louvain")   
```

### Plot of the comparison

- The horizontal axis shows how much we perturb the network. 

- The vertical axis shows Variation of Information, which measures the difference between two partitions. A lower VI means that the communities have changed less. By comparing the curves, we can see which method is more stable under these perturbations.

Louvain communities are more stable, becasuse its curve has a lower VI index. 
```{r}
plot(comparison)
```


## Robustness of the network communities

Are <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Louvain communities</strong></span> more robust than the <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>randomized reference network</strong></span>?

- Creation of the randomized graph using `random()`.
```{r}

graphRandom <- robin::random(
  graph = graph,
  dist = "Other"
)

```

`robinRobust()` compares the robustness behavior with that reference.
Comparison between null model and Louvain model
```{r}
robust <- robinRobust(graph=graph, graphRandom=graphRandom, method="louvain") 
```

Plot of the comparison:

- Louvain communities are better.
```{r}
plot(robust)
```

# Alternative Graph construction

We can build another network from the same data using a different similarity measure, like <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>Cosine similarity</strong></span>, which compares the directions of patient expression vectors. 

```{r, warning=FALSE}
library(lsa)

rna_data <- rna_filtered[, 2:372]

rna_cosine_similarity <- lsa::cosine(
  as.matrix(rna_data)
)

diag(rna_cosine_similarity) <- 0 # No self-loops
```

## Creation od edgelist

As with the Pearson network, the cosine similarity is simmetric. We take just one triangle of the matrix to avoid repeated pairs. Then, we create a table with the two patient names and their cosine similarity. This is the edge list for our second network.

```{r}
edge_index_cosine <- which(
  lower.tri(rna_cosine_similarity, diag = FALSE),
  arr.ind = TRUE
)

rna_cosine_all_edges <- data.frame(
  from = colnames(rna_cosine_similarity)[edge_index_cosine[, 1]],
  to = colnames(rna_cosine_similarity)[edge_index_cosine[, 2]],
  weight = rna_cosine_similarity[edge_index_cosine]
)

head(rna_cosine_all_edges)
```

## Similarity threshold

We do not want to connect every patient to every other patient. We calculate the 85th percentile of the cosine similarities and keep the values above that threshold. 

```{r}
cosine_similarities <- rna_cosine_similarity[
  lower.tri(rna_cosine_similarity)
]

threshold_cosine <- quantile(
  cosine_similarities,
  0.85,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

```

Keep only similarities above the threshold.
```{r}
rna_cosine_adjacency <- rna_cosine_similarity

rna_cosine_adjacency[
  rna_cosine_adjacency < threshold_cosine
] <- 0

diag(rna_cosine_adjacency) <- 0
```

Graph construction:
```{r}
rna_cosine_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
  rna_cosine_adjacency,
  mode = "upper",
  diag = FALSE,
  weighted = TRUE
)

rna_cosine_graph <- delete_edges(
  rna_cosine_graph,
  E(rna_cosine_graph)[E(rna_cosine_graph)$weight == 0]
)
```

# Distribution comparison

We compare the edge weights of the 2 networks and show the two distributions side by side.
```{r}
#Edge weights
df_weights <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    Weight = E(rna_graph)$weight,
    Method = "Pearson"
  ),
  data.frame(
    Weight = E(rna_cosine_graph)$weight,
    Method = "Cosine"
  )
)

#Density plots
ggplot(df_weights, aes(x = Weight, fill = Method)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(~ Method, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Pearson" = "#377EB8",
    "Cosine" = "#E69F00"
  )) +
  labs(
    x = "Edge weight",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of edge weights"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  )
```

# A different network analysis

We can build a different network anayalis, with a differnt aim.

- The <span style="color:#B22222;"><strong>nodes are genes:</strong></span>, and we compare their expression patterns across patients. 

We randomly select 500 genes to keep the example small enough to explore during the workshop.
```{r, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
n_genes <- nrow(data_rna)
selected_indices <- sample(1:n_genes, 500)
rna_sample <- data_rna[selected_indices, ]

gene_names <- as.character(rna_sample$attrib_name)
rna_sample <- as.matrix(rna_sample[, -1])
rownames(rna_sample) <- gene_names
```

## Pearson correlation between genes

We calculate Pearson correlations between genes instead of patients. 
- The `cor()` function compares columns of a matrix. 

- `t()` transpose the matrix before calculating the correlations. This gives us a gene-by-gene similarity matrix.

```{r}
rna_similarity <- cor(t(rna_sample))
diag(rna_similarity) <- 0
```

Using the same functions as in the previous steps, we can construct a gene similarity network.
```{r}
# Edge indices
edge_index <- which(
  lower.tri(rna_similarity, diag = FALSE),
  arr.ind = TRUE
)

# Edge list
rna_all_edges <- data.frame(
  from = rownames(rna_sample)[edge_index[, 1]],
  to = rownames(rna_sample)[edge_index[, 2]],
  weight = rna_similarity[edge_index]
)
```

# 85th percentile threshold

Just as before, we calculate the 85th percentile of the gene correlations and set smaller values to zero. 
```{r}
threshold <- quantile(
  rna_similarity[lower.tri(rna_similarity)],
  0.85,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

rna_adjacency <- rna_similarity
rna_adjacency[rna_adjacency < threshold] <- 0
diag(rna_adjacency) <- 0
```


# Weighted graph

We can now turn the gene adjacency matrix into an `igraph` object. 

```{r}
rna_graph <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
  rna_adjacency,
  mode = "upper",
  diag = FALSE,
  weighted = TRUE
)

rna_graph
```

## Network characteristics

With igraph we can study different Network characteristics.


Number of nodes and edges:
```{r}
vcount(rna_graph)

ecount(rna_graph)
```

Network density:
```{r}
edge_density(rna_graph)
```

Global clustering coefficient:
```{r}
transitivity(rna_graph, type = "global")
```

Number of isolated nodes:
```{r}
sum(degree(rna_graph) == 0)
```

## Node charactestistics
Node degree:
```{r}
node_degree <- degree(rna_graph)
```

Betweenness centrality:
```{r}
node_betweenness <- betweenness(
  rna_graph,
  directed = FALSE,
  weights = NA
)
```

Closeness centrality
```{r}
node_closeness <- closeness(
  rna_graph,
  mode = "all",
  weights = NA,
  normalized = TRUE
)
```

Hub centrality
```{r}
node_hub <- hub_score(
  rna_graph,
  weights = NA
)$vector

```


We can build a dataframe:
```{r}
node_metrics <- data.frame(
  Gene = rownames(rna_sample),
  Degree = node_degree,
  Betweenness = node_betweenness,
  Closeness = node_closeness, 
  Hub_Centrality = node_hub
)

head(node_metrics)
```

## Edge characteristics

As nodes, we can study the properites of the connections.

Edge betweenness centrality:
```{r}
edge_betweenness_values <- edge_betweenness(
  rna_graph,
  directed = FALSE,
  weights = NA
)
```

Edge weights:
```{r}
edge_weights <- E(rna_graph)$weight
```

We can build a second dataframe:
```{r}
edge_list <- as_data_frame(rna_graph, what = "edges")

edge_metrics <- data.frame(
  Gene_1 = edge_list$from,
  Gene_2 = edge_list$to,
  Weight = edge_weights,
  Edge_Betweenness = edge_betweenness_values
)

head(edge_metrics)
```
